book.title: Big Magic: Creative Living Beyond Fear
book.author: Elizabeth Gilbert

confidence_note: This entry overlaps with story 1179 (inspiration as a visitor). To avoid repeating the Ruth Stone story, it uses another anecdote Gilbert tells about the musician Tom Waits: driving on a Los Angeles freeway, he felt a fragment of a song arrive, had no way to write it down, and at first panicked; then he spoke to the song, saying something like 'Can't you see I'm driving?' and suggesting it come back at a better time or go bother someone else, such as Leonard Cohen. The anxiety eased; he felt the creative process was a collaboration, not his sole burden. The story is widely told, including in Gilbert's TED talk; wording is paraphrased.
facts: Gilbert tells a story about the musician Tom Waits.
Waits was driving on a Los Angeles freeway when he heard a fragment of a melody in his head, the beginning of a song.
He had no paper, no pen, no recorder. He felt the familiar panic of an artist who is about to lose an idea.

Then he did something unusual. He looked up and spoke to the song, telling it he was driving and couldn't take it down right now; if it wanted to exist, it could come back at a better moment, or go and bother someone else, like Leonard Cohen.
His anxiety eased. He realized that the creative process didn't have to be a torment he carried alone; it could be a strange, even humorous collaboration.
Gilbert uses this to argue that creators can relate to inspiration more lightly, without letting it rule them through fear.
tension: A song arrives at the worst possible moment. Panic, or conversation?
opening_idea: Tom Waits is driving on the freeway when a song arrives in his head, and he has nothing to write it down with.

lessons.idea: You don't have to carry creativity alone.

lessons.anchor: Telling it to go bother someone else

reflect: What happens in you when an idea arrives at the wrong moment?
Where could you take your creative work a little less anxiously?
reflect_final: How would you treat your ideas if they were collaborators, not bosses?

use_cases.situation: Ideas come to you at inconvenient moments and you panic about losing them.
use_cases.move: Keep a simple capture tool, and when you can't, trust that good ideas return.

use_cases.situation: A team member is anxious about producing a brilliant idea on demand.
use_cases.move: Take the pressure off: ideas often arrive in their own time.

use_cases.situation: Your child gets frustrated when inspiration for a drawing won't come.
use_cases.move: Suggest they tell the idea to come back later and go play for a while.

pocket_idea: Treat inspiration as a collaborator, not a tyrant.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Tom Waits told a song that arrived while he was driving to go bother Leonard Cohen instead.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Freeway, song fragment, panic, talking to the song, lighter creative life.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What happens when an idea arrives at the wrong moment?
